info.description: Inbound trucks. Each truck is an ENTITY carrying its load: the pallets are created, batched into one truck, and the truck leaves by "trucks" -- link it to a Dock's "in" port, where it holds a door until it is empty. That is what makes truck turnaround, door time per truck and trucks waiting real KPIs instead of pallet-level averages. Trucks come on an interarrival time or on a named arrival schedule (trucks per period). Place one instance per product stream: the mix is visible on the palette and each stream keeps its own routing, its own load size and its own rate. The pallets' routing starts AFTER the dock -- the truck brings them there.

info.description: A receiving dock: a number of doors, and a crew shared with the rest of the site. A TRUCK arrives at a door, holds it for its whole stay, is unloaded pallet by pallet by one member of the crew, and its pallets leave by "out" on their own routing. Door time is therefore per truck, not per pallet, and the truck's own time in system is its turnaround. The dock is a STATION and brings its own network node, so put it where the doors really are and draw an aisle to it.

info.description: A rack zone with a finite number of pallet positions. A pallet claims a position when it arrives -- and WAITS in the aisle if the zone is full, which is what makes "Time Full %" and the zone's average occupancy real KPIs -- and is put away. What happens next is the MODE. "stock": the pallet's journey ends in the rack as stock, and an Order picking instance bound to this zone's level draws it out later, which is the order-driven warehouse. "pass_through": the pallet dwells for a sampled time and leaves by "out", carrying its own position back with it -- the original behaviour, for a model with no order stream. The zone is a routed STATION with its own network node, and its pallet positions are a level, so a fill indicator draws how full the racking is.

parameters.label: Zone mode
parameters.help: pass_through: a pallet dwells for the sampled time below and leaves by "out". stock: it stays in the rack as stock and nothing leaves by "out" -- an Order picking instance whose "Zone stock" names THIS instance's level (<this block>/Log Zone stock) takes it out when a customer order asks for it. The dwell parameters are ignored in stock mode.

parameters.label: Opening stock

info.description: A stream of customer orders: one order at a time on a mean interval, or an arrival schedule for a day whose order intake has a shape. Each order is stamped with its number of LINES (entity.log_lines) and the stock it needs (entity.log_qty = lines x units per line), which is what an Order picking station reads. Give it a promised lead time and it also stamps entity.due_date, so the run reports a service level against it. No input port -- this asset starts the outbound flow.

info.description: The outbound half of an order-driven warehouse: an order arrives, DRAWS its quantity from a storage zone's stock, and is picked. Name the zone's own level in "Zone stock" -- a Storage zone instance called zone_a owns "zone_a/Log Zone stock" -- and this station empties the racking another asset fills, with no wiring between the two. An order the zone cannot fill WAITS as a backorder and is served the exact instant a put-away brings the stock up, so "Log fill rate" (the share served straight from stock) and "Log backorder time" are the two service numbers a warehouse is judged on. Pick time is a fixed part per order plus a part per line, exactly as the Picking station's is; use THAT asset instead when pallets flow through the racking rather than being drawn from it.

info.description: A belt between two points on the floor. Capacity is floor(length / spacing) and travel is length / speed, both exact. A belt only backs up against something the model can name: give it the resource at its far end (the loaders, the wrapper, a Picking station's picker pool) and an accumulating belt packs pallets against the stop while a non-accumulating one stops dead. The end stop may belong to ANOTHER asset -- a shared pool by its plain name, or one asset's own scoped resource as "<instance>/<resource>". The asset brings both of its endpoints as network nodes; drag the far one to where the belt really ends. Name the station at its head and the belt becomes a routing step in its own right, so a vehicle delivers onto it.

parameters.name: station_name
parameters.label: Station at the head
parameters.help: Name this belt as a routing STEP and a vehicle can deliver onto it: the pallet is carried to the head of the belt and rides from there. Empty leaves the belt an ordinary linked block.

parameters.name: accumulating
parameters.label: Accumulating
parameters.help: On: a blocked pallet's followers pack against it and the belt keeps loading. Off: the whole belt stops until the far end clears.

parameters.name: exit_resource
parameters.label: End stop
parameters.help: The resource a pallet must take a unit of before it may leave the belt -- the usual pairing is a PROCESS with action "Delay Release" at the far end, which is what a Picking station does with "Picker taken" set to Delay Release. A resource owned by another asset instance is written "<instance>/<resource>". Empty means a free-running belt that never blocks.

info.description: The outbound end: pallets are consolidated into truck loads, the load is loaded through one of the dock's doors, and the pallets leave again as themselves -- so pallet counts, costs and DUE DATES all survive the batch. A load goes out when it is full or when the cut-off time since its first pallet passes, whichever comes first; a cut-off of 0 means a truck only ever leaves full.

info.description: The vehicles that carry pallets between stations, and the ONE block that moves them. Wire every station's exit into this asset's "in" port: the vehicle drives empty to the pallet, loads it, drives it to the pallet's next routing step and unloads. A model needs one of these per fleet, not one per station -- a second instance is a second fleet (AGVs beside forklifts), not a second mover block. Distances come from the path network, so the answer to "should the dock move" is geometry rather than a guess.

info.title: Order-driven warehouse (library assets)
info.description: An order-driven warehouse built from the Logistics library alone: inbound trucks, a receiving dock, forklifts putting pallets away into two rack zones that HOLD them as stock, customer orders drawing that stock with backorders when it is short, order picking, a take-away belt and an outbound dock that consolidates truck loads. Inbound and outbound are two entity streams that meet at each zone's level; each asset brought its own network node when it was placed, and the aisles joining them are the only geometry drawn by hand.
info.author: Naga
info.notes: Metres, minutes, metres per minute. Fast movers and bulk pallets have their own zone, their own order stream and their own picking station, so a shortage in one is visible on its own fill rate. The zones open with about half their positions filled and the two streams are sized to roughly balance, which is what makes the demand-surge scenario a real question rather than a foregone conclusion.
